title: Frobenius Groups and the Normal Complement Theorem

items.title: Frobenius complement and frobenius group
items.statement: For a finite group G, a subgroup 1<H<G is a Frobenius complement if H∩gHg^{-1}=1 for every g∉H; then G is a Frobenius group with complement H.
items.proof_plan: Define conjugation convention gHg^{-1}; exclude H=1 and H=G.

references.title: Alex Bartel, Introduction to Representation Theory of Finite Groups, §6.1

items.strategy: Define conjugation convention gHg^{-1}; exclude H=1 and H=G.

items.title: Frobenius permutation action characterization
items.statement: The complement condition for 1<H<G is equivalent to the left action of G on G/H being transitive, nonregular, and having every nonidentity element fix at most one coset.
items.proof_plan: Stabilizer of gH is gHg^{-1}. Two distinct cosets have different conjugate stabilizers, and their common stabilizer is trivial exactly by the complement condition. Nontrivial H ensures a nonidentity point stabilizer.

references.title: Alex Bartel, Introduction to Representation Theory of Finite Groups, §6.1
Hans Kurzweil and Bernd Stellmacher, The Theory of Finite Groups, §§7.1–7.2

items.title: Frobenius kernel set
items.statement: For a Frobenius complement H define the candidate kernel set N={1}∪(G\⋃_{g∈G}gHg^{-1}); no subgroup property is presumed.
items.proof_plan: The set consists of the identity and elements with no fixed point in the coset action; normality under conjugation is only setwise, not closure under products.

references.title: Alex Bartel, Introduction to Representation Theory of Finite Groups, §6.1

items.title: Frobenius kernel cardinality
items.statement: For the candidate set N, |N|=[G:H] and N∩H=1.
items.proof_plan: The Frobenius condition makes N_G(H)=H, so there are [G:H] distinct conjugates. Their nonidentity parts are disjoint, giving |⋃H^g|=1+[G:H](|H|−1), hence |N|=[G:H]. The defining complement gives N∩H=1.

items.title: Induced class functions and restricted class functions
items.statement: For a finite group G, a subgroup H, and a class function theta on H, the induced class function Ind_H^G theta on G is defined by the Frobenius formula, is C-linear in theta, and agrees with the induced character when theta is a character; Res_H^G is restriction of class functions.
items.proof_plan: Define Ind by the Frobenius formula on class functions; verify class-function property, C-linearity and agreement with honest characters. Register as a local supplier for the virtual-character route.

references.title: Alex Bartel, Introduction to Representation Theory of Finite Groups, §6.1
Peter Webb, A Course in Finite Group Representation Theory, §4.3

items.strategy: Define Ind by the Frobenius formula on class functions; verify the three elementary properties.

items.title: Frobenius reciprocity for class functions
items.statement: For a finite group G, a subgroup H, a class function theta on H and a class function psi on G, <Ind_H^G theta, psi>_G = <theta, Res_H^G psi>_H.
items.proof_plan: Expand theta and psi in their orthonormal bases of irreducible characters, use linearity/conjugate-linearity of the inner product and honest-character Frobenius reciprocity.

references.title: Alex Bartel, Introduction to Representation Theory of Finite Groups, §6.1

items.title: Zero at identity induction restriction for a frobenius complement
items.statement: If θ is a complex class function on H with θ(1)=0, then Res_H^G Ind_H^G θ=θ.
items.proof_plan: Use the induced-character formula at h∈H. For h≠1 a conjugate xhx^{-1} in H forces x∈H by malnormality; the |H| terms then each equal θ(h). At h=1 every term vanishes. Extend the formula linearly from characters to class functions.

items.title: Frobenius character extension construction
items.statement: For nontrivial φ∈Irr(H), put θ=φ−φ(1)1_H and φ̃=Ind_H^G θ+φ(1)1_G. Then φ̃|_H=φ, φ̃(1)=φ(1), and φ̃(g)=φ(1) for g outside all conjugates of H.
items.proof_plan: Apply zero-at-identity restriction to θ. On elements outside conjugates, the induced class function is zero by the induced formula; at 1 the induced term is zero because θ(1)=0. This construction is initially a virtual character; genuineness follows in the next lemma.

items.title: Frobenius character extension is irreducible
items.statement: For every nontrivial φ∈Irr(H), the constructed φ̃ is an irreducible character of G.
items.proof_plan: Frobenius reciprocity and the restriction lemma give <Ind θ,Ind θ>=<θ,θ>=1+φ(1)^2 and <Ind θ,1_G>=−φ(1). Hence <φ̃,φ̃>=1. As φ̃ is an integral virtual character, its irreducible coefficients are integers with squares summing to 1, so φ̃=±χ for a genuine irreducible χ. The positive value φ̃(1)=φ(1) rules out the minus sign.

items.title: Frobenius kernel is an intersection of character kernels
items.statement: N=⋂_{φ∈Irr(H),φ≠1_H} ker φ̃, with the empty intersection interpreted as G only when H=1 (excluded here).
items.proof_plan: Each g∈N has φ̃(g)=φ̃(1), hence lies in every kernel. The intersection M is normal as an intersection of representation kernels and M∩H=1 since irreducible characters of H jointly separate H. For any normal M with M∩H=1, every M-element lies outside all nonidentity conjugate-H elements, so M⊆N. Thus equality; no closure of N was assumed.

items.title: Frobenius kernel theorem
items.statement: For a finite Frobenius group with complement H, the candidate kernel set N is a normal subgroup of G.
items.proof_plan: Use the preceding exact intersection of kernels of genuine representations. Normality of each kernel and their intersection proves subgroup closure and normality; the cardinality lemma is not used to infer closure.

items.title: Frobenius semidirect product decomposition
items.statement: For the normal Frobenius kernel N, G=N⋊H, |N|=[G:H], and N is the unique normal complement made of the identity and fixed-point-free elements of the coset action.
items.proof_plan: The counting lemma gives |N||H|=|G| and N∩H=1. Since N is normal, NH is a subgroup of full order, so G=NH. The defining fixed-point-free set is fixed by the given action and therefore unique.

items.title: Frobenius groups and fixed point free actions
items.statement: If G=N⋊H is Frobenius with 1<N and 1<H, each 1≠h∈H fixes only 1 in N. Conversely, if finite nontrivial N and H form N⋊H and H acts fixed-point-freely on N\{1}, then H is a Frobenius complement.
items.proof_plan: Write any g∉H as nh. Conjugate intersections reduce to H∩nHn^{-1}; a nonidentity common element exists exactly when a nonidentity h∈H centralizes n, using N∩H=1. This proves both directions with the nontrivial hypotheses explicit.

Hans Kurzweil and Bernd Stellmacher, The Theory of Finite Groups, §§7.1–7.2

items.title: The p-prime core of a finite group
items.statement: O_{p'}(G) is the unique largest normal p'-subgroup of a finite group G: the subgroup generated by all normal p'-subgroups, which is itself normal of order prime to p and contains every normal p'-subgroup.

references.title: Paul Flavell, An Introduction to Transfer and Fusion in Finite Groups, §§2–5
Hans Kurzweil and Bernd Stellmacher, The Theory of Finite Groups, §§7.1–7.2

items.title: Normal p complement and p nilpotent group
items.statement: For finite G and prime p, a normal p-complement is K◁G with p∤|K| and [G:K] a p-power; equivalently G=K⋊P for any P∈Syl_p(G). G is p-nilpotent when such K exists.
items.proof_plan: Given K, the Sylow order equals [G:K], so K∩P=1 and KP=G; conversely semidirect form gives the Hall p-prime property. Include P=1 and K=G.

items.title: Transfer homomorphism for a finite index subgroup
items.statement: For finite G, H≤G, φ:H→A with A abelian, and representatives t_α∈α of right cosets α=Ht_α, define V_φ(x)=∏_{α∈H\G}φ(t_α x t_{α x}^{−1}).
items.proof_plan: The index αx means the right action on right cosets. Each factor lies in H; A being abelian makes the product order irrelevant. Independence and homomorphism are separate lemmas.

items.statement: For x,y∈G, V_φ(xy)=V_φ(x)V_φ(y).

items.title: Transfer cycle decomposition formula
items.statement: If right multiplication by x on H\G has cycles of lengths n_i with representatives Ht_i, then V_φ(x)=∏_i φ(t_i x^{n_i}t_i^{-1}).
items.proof_plan: Choose the transversal along each cycle as t_i,t_ix,…,t_ix^{n_i−1}. All factors except the final one in each cycle equal 1; the final factor is t_i x^{n_i}t_i^{-1}∈H. Use transversal independence.

items.title: Equivalent forms of having a normal p complement
items.statement: For finite G, normal p-complement is equivalent to a normal p′ subgroup of p-power index, an epimorphism G→P onto a Sylow p-subgroup, or closure under products of all p′-elements. Under these conditions the complement is O_{p′}(G), the largest normal p′ subgroup, and is precisely the set of p′-elements.
items.proof_plan: A normal complement is its own p′-core. Quotient by a normal p′ subgroup of p-power index is isomorphic to P. An epimorphism onto P has p′ kernel and kills every p′ element. Product closure plus inverses makes the p′-elements a characteristic subgroup; its order contains every non-p Sylow order, so it is a normal p-complement. Include G=1 and P=1.

items.title: P residual of a finite group
items.statement: O^p(G) is the intersection of all normal subgroups N◁G for which G/N is a p-group, the least normal subgroup with p-group quotient.
items.proof_plan: There are finitely many normal subgroups; the diagonal embedding of G/(N₁∩N₂) in (G/N₁)×(G/N₂) shows the intersection again has p-group quotient.

items.title: Sylow subgroups of a normal subgroup are intersections with Sylow subgroups
items.statement: If K is a normal subgroup of the finite group G and P is a Sylow p-subgroup of G, then K∩P is a Sylow p-subgroup of K; if in addition [G:K] is a power of p, then G=KP.

references.title: Paul Flavell, An Introduction to Transfer and Fusion in Finite Groups, §§2–5
Hans Kurzweil and Bernd Stellmacher, The Theory of Finite Groups, §§7.1–7.2

items.proof_plan: Conjugate a Sylow of K into P and compare orders; additivity of the index gives KP=G when [G:K] is a p-power.

items.title: P residual is generated by p prime elements and idempotent
items.statement: For finite G, O^p(G) is generated by all p′-elements; G=P O^p(G) for every Sylow P; and O^p(O^p(G))=O^p(G).
items.proof_plan: Every homomorphism to a p-group kills p′ elements, so their generated normal subgroup lies in O^p(G). Its quotient has only p-elements and is therefore a p-group (Cauchy), giving the reverse inclusion. Sylow orders imply G=P O^p(G). All p′ generators of O^p(G) remain p′ there, proving idempotence.

items.title: Abelian sylow fusion in its normalizer
items.statement: If P∈Syl_p(G) is abelian and x,y∈P are G-conjugate, then they are N_G(P)-conjugate.
items.proof_plan: If x^g=y, then P and P^g lie in C_G(y), where each is a Sylow p-subgroup because already Sylow in G. Choose c∈C_G(y) with P^{gc}=P by Sylow conjugacy. Then x^{gc}=y.

items.title: Burnside normal p complement theorem
items.statement: If P∈Syl_p(G) and P≤Z(N_G(P)), then G has a normal p-complement.
items.proof_plan: P is abelian. Transfer from G through P via identity φ:P→P. Each cycle contribution for x∈P is a G-conjugate in P of x^{n_i}; by abelian-Sylow fusion it is N_G(P)-conjugate, hence equals x^{n_i} because P centralizes N_G(P). Thus V(x)=x^{[G:P]}. Since [G:P] is coprime to |P|, the power map is bijective on P, so transfer surjects to P. Its kernel is normal p′ of index |P|.

items.statement: P controls its own element fusion if for x,y∈P, G-conjugacy of x and y implies P-conjugacy.

items.title: Proper subgroup of a finite p group is properly normalized local
items.statement: If S is a proper subgroup of a finite p-group P, then S<N_P(S).

items.title: Normal p complements pass to subgroups and p local normalizers
items.statement: If G has a normal p-complement K, every subgroup H≤G and every quotient G/L has one; in particular N_G(Q) has one for each nontrivial p-subgroup Q.

items.title: Fusion control and centralizer transitivity are equivalent
items.statement:
Let $H$ be a finite group, $p$ a prime, and $P\in\operatorname{Syl}_p(H)$
(def-sylow-p-subgroup). The following are equivalent.

(i) $N_H(P)$ controls fusion in $P$ with respect to $H$: whenever $x,y\in P$ and
$y=hxh^{-1}$ for some $h\in H$, there is $u\in N_H(P)$ with $y=uxu^{-1}$.
(ii) For every $x\in P$ with $x\ne e$, the centralizer
$C_H(x)=\{h\in H:hx=xh\}$ acts by conjugation transitively on the set
$\operatorname{Syl}_p(H;x):=\{T\in\operatorname{Syl}_p(H):x\in T\}$ of Sylow
$p$-subgroups of $H$ containing $x$; that is, for any $T_1,T_2\in\operatorname{Syl}_p(H;x)$ there is $c\in C_H(x)$ with $T_2=T_1^{c}=cT_1c^{-1}$.

references.title: Paul Flavell, An Introduction to Transfer and Fusion in Finite Groups, §§2–5
Hans Kurzweil and Bernd Stellmacher, The Theory of Finite Groups, §§7.1–7.2

items.proof_plan: Both directions are elementary conjugacy adjustments: transport a Sylow conjugator by an element of the normalizer, respectively by an element of the centralizer, using Sylow II.

items.title: Local sylow conjugacy ascent for fusion
items.statement: Suppose that for every nontrivial p-subgroup S≤P and every nonidentity x∈S, C_{N_G(S)}(x) acts transitively on the Sylow p-subgroups of N_G(S) containing x. Then N_G(P) controls fusion in P.
items.proof_plan: For x≠1 and Sylow Q,R containing x, induct downward on |Q∩R|. If Q≠R, S=Q∩R contains x and is proper in both. Proper-subgroup normalizer gives N_Q(S),N_R(S)>S. Choose Sylows T_Q,T_R of N_G(S) over them and extend to Sylows Q*,R* of G. The local centralizer-transitivity hypothesis gives c∈C_{N_G(S)}(x) carrying T_Q to T_R. Then Q∩Q*, R∩R*, and (Q*)^c∩R* strictly contain S, so induction chains the Sylows by C_G(x). Finally centralizer transitivity in G gives N_G(P)-fusion control.

items.title: Local normal p complements force control of fusion
items.statement: If every N_G(Q), 1≠Q≤P, has a normal p-complement, then P controls its own element fusion.

items.title: Normal p subgroup has proper commutator in a p group
items.statement: If 1≠Q◁P with P a finite p-group, then [Q,P]<Q.
items.proof_plan: Choose a maximal P-normal T<Q. In P/T, the nontrivial normal p-subgroup Q/T intersects the center nontrivially by counting its conjugation orbits modulo p. Minimality forces Q/T to be central, hence [Q,P]≤T<Q. Also Q′≤[Q,P], so Q/[Q,P] is nontrivial abelian.

items.title: Fusion control gives a nontrivial p quotient of the p residual
items.statement: If P controls fusion and K=O^p(G) has nontrivial Sylow Q=P∩K, then transfer K→Q/[Q,P] is nontrivial; this contradicts O^p(K)=K.
items.proof_plan: Q◁P and [Q,P]<Q, so A=Q/[Q,P] is a nontrivial abelian p-group. Form transfer on K via Q→A. For x∈Q, each cycle contribution is K-conjugate to x^{n_i} and lies in Q⊂P; fusion control makes it P-conjugate to x^{n_i}, equal in A because Q◁P and [Q,P] is killed. Thus V(x)=x^{[K:Q]} in A, with exponent prime to p, so V is nontrivial and surjective. But every map K→p-group kills O^p(K)=K.

items.title: Frobenius normal p complement theorem
items.statement: For finite G and P∈Syl_p(G), the following are equivalent: G has a normal p-complement; every N_G(Q) for 1≠Q≤P has one; and P controls its own element fusion.
items.proof_plan: Global→local is inheritance; local→fusion is the local fusion lemma. For fusion→global, if P=1 take K=G. Otherwise K=O^p(G) and G=PK. If K had p-divisible order, Q=P∩K is nontrivial and the p-residual transfer lemma contradicts O^p(K)=K. Thus K is p′ and G/K is a p-group, making K the required normal p-complement.

items.title: The local automizer condition gives centralizer conjugacy of Sylow subgroups
items.statement: Let H be finite, p prime and S≤H a nontrivial p-subgroup. Set N=N_H(S), C=C_H(S). If N/C is a p-group, then C acts transitively on the Sylow p-subgroups of N; for every x∈S, C_N(x) is transitive on those Sylow p-subgroups containing x.

items.title: P automizer condition implies fusion control
items.statement: If N_G(Q)/C_G(Q) is a p-group for every 1≠Q≤P, then P controls its own element fusion.
items.proof_plan: The condition is conjugacy-invariant, so applies to any nontrivial p-subgroup S. For each S≤P and x∈S nontrivial, put N=N_G(S), C=C_G(S). items.title: Affine linear frobenius groups over finite fields
items.statement: For every finite field F_q with q>2, F_q⋊F_q^× acting on F_q by x↦ax+b is Frobenius; its kernel is the translation group and its complement the nontrivial multiplicative group.

items.title: Right translation scales left haar measure
items.statement: Assume AC. For a fixed left Haar measure μ on an LCH group G and g∈G, f↦∫f(xg)dμ(x) is integration against a left Haar measure, hence equals a unique positive scalar c(g)∫f dμ on C_c(G).

items.title: Counting measure on a discrete group is Haar, Haar measures there are its multiples, and integrals against them are sums
items.statement: Let G be an LCH group with the discrete topology. Then counting measure #_G on P(G) is a left Haar measure and a right Haar measure; every left Haar measure mu on G equals c*#_G with c = mu({e}) > 0 uniquely determined; and for every nonnegative finite-valued H one has int_G H dmu = c sum_{y in G} H(y), while every mu-integrable complex H satisfies the same identity with sum_y |H(y)| < infinity.
items.proof_plan: Discreteness makes every subset open and Borel, makes compact sets finite and turns inner regularity into a supremum over finite sets, so counting measure is a nonzero invariant Radon measure; the same computation identifies an arbitrary left Haar measure as mu({e})*counting; the integral formula follows by comparing the supremum over simple minorants with the supremum of the finite subsums, and the complex case by splitting into positive and negative parts.

items.statement: Assume AC. There is a net (e_U)⊂C_c(G), indexed by identity neighbourhoods, with e_U≥0, supp e_U⊂U, ||e_U||₁=1, and ||e_U*f−f||₁, ||f*e_U−f||₁→0 for every f∈L¹(G).

items.title: L1 group algebra has a unit iff g is discrete
items.statement: Assume AC. L¹(G) has a convolution identity exactly when G is discrete; for discrete G with Haar μ=c·counting, the identity is c^{-1}1_{ {e} }.

For f∈C_c, u*f is continuous: approximate u by C_c in L1 and use the uniform estimate ||(u−v)*f||∞≤||u−v||₁||f||∞. Equality u*f=f a.e. then holds everywhere because Haar has full support. At e, f(e)=∫u(y)f(y^{-1})dμ(y). If G were nondiscrete, μ({e})=0 by compact finiteness and translation invariance; outer regularity gives arbitrarily small neighbourhoods V of e. Choose f∈C_c supported V^{-1}, 0≤f≤1, f(e)=1; then the displayed identity at e gives 1≤∫_V|u|<1, a contradiction.

items.title: Left and right regular unitary representations
items.statement: Assume AC and fix left Haar μ. On L²(G,μ) define λ(g)ξ(x)=ξ(g^{-1}x) and ρ(g)ξ(x)=Δ_G(g)^{1/2}ξ(xg).

items.statement: Assume AC. Both λ and ρ are strongly continuous unitary representations of G on L²(G), and λ is faithful as a group representation.

items.title: Modular function of the affine group of the line
items.statement: Assuming AC, for G={(a,b):a>0,b∈R} with (a,b)(a′,b′)=(aa′,b+ab′), left Haar is a^{-2}da db and Δ_G(a,b)=a^{-1}; thus G is nonunimodular.
items.proof_plan: Left multiplication has Jacobian a₀² and sends a to a₀a, so a^{-2}da db is left invariant. Right multiplication by (a₀,b₀) has Jacobian a₀; substitution in the defining integral gives factor a₀=Δ(g^{-1}). The subgroup a>0 suffices and avoids the disconnected-sign convention.

items.title: Convolution on a discrete group
items.statement: Assume AC. For a discrete group G with Haar measure μ=c·counting, the L1 involution is f*(x)=overline{f(x^{-1})}, convolution is the absolutely convergent series (f*g)(x)=c∑_y f(y)g(y^{-1}x), and c^{-1}1_{ {e} } is its norm-one two-sided unit, also when G is uncountable.

Prove the series is absolutely convergent and L1-bounded by finite-subsum estimates, then identify it with the L1 convolution by density. Directly compute the unit and involution from discrete unimodularity.

items.title: Convolution on a compact group
items.statement: Assume AC. With normalized Haar on compact G, 1*1=1. For finite-dimensional irreducible unitary π,σ and first-variable-linear coefficients, the convolution is zero if they are inequivalent; if T:W→V is a unitary intertwiner, it is (⟨u,Tz⟩/dim π) f^π_{Tw,v}, independent of T.
items.proof_plan: Under AC, use normalized Haar, L1/L2 density and strong continuity to identify the coefficient convolution with the pointwise integral. Form the averaged intertwiner, use irreducibility and an eigenvalue to show it is zero for inequivalent representations and scalar times any unitary intertwiner otherwise. Compute the scalar by a rank-one trace and verify independence of the intertwiner; the constant function has convolution square one.

items.statement: Assuming AC, on the positive affine group, the map Jf(x)=overline{f(x^{-1})} without Δ is not an isometry of L¹(G).
